title: Mitigating Sequential Reappearance in Diffusion Data-Point Unlearning

paper.title: Mitigating Sequential Reappearance in Diffusion Data-Point Unlearning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion data-point unlearning is typically evaluated immediately after each deletion, even though subsequent requests may repeatedly update the same model. We identify sequential reappearance, a failure mode in which an instance that is initially judged to be forgotten later returns to the memorized regime without reuse of the deleted data or adversarial fine-tuning. To capture this behavior, we introduce a target-level evaluation protocol that tracks whether each target is forgotten immediately, remains forgotten at the end of the sequence, or reappears during subsequent deletions. We further find that targets that later reappear exhibit sharper local denoising-loss geometry after deletion than targets that remain forgotten.
We characterize this vulnerability as data-space recovery sharpness and show that this post-deletion local geometry is associated with subsequent reappearance risk.
Motivated by this finding, we propose a sharpness-guided unlearning method that iteratively identifies the most recoverable region around each target and extends the deletion objective to that region. Experiments show that our method improves forgetting persistence across long deletion sequences while preserving generation utility, highlighting the importance of evaluating diffusion unlearning beyond immediate deletion efficacy.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Sequential reappearance in CelebA-HQ. (a) Outputs generated immediately after unlearning each target and after processing all subsequent deletion requests. Existing methods can reproduce initially forgotten targets in the final model, whereas LASTING maintains forgetting throughout the sequence. (b) Number of reappeared images as sequential deletion requests accumulate. Diffusion models can memorize and reproduce individual training examples, raising privacy and copyright concerns when sensitive data must be removed ( Somepalli et al. 2023a ; Carlini et al. 2023 ) . Diffusion data-point unlearning addresses this problem by removing the influence of a specific training instance without retraining the model from scratch ( Alberti et al. 2025 ; Shi et al. 2026 ) . A reliable deletion, however, should remain effective not only when it is performed but also throughout subsequent updates to the same model. As illustrated in Figure 1(a) , a target that appears successfully forgotten at its immediate checkpoint can become memorized again after later deletion requests are processed. Existing evaluations of diffusion unlearning ( Alberti et al. 2025 ; Wu et al. 2025 ; Shi et al. 2026 ; Park and Park 2026 ) predominantly assess each target at or near the model state immediately following its deletion. Such stage-local evaluation overlooks the target’s lifecycle under future model updates and can therefore overestimate deletion reliability. We identify sequential reappearance , a failure mode in which an initially forgotten target returns to the memorized regime as subsequent deletion requests update the model. Importantly, this failure emerges within the ordinary unlearning sequence, without reusing the deleted target, adversarially fine-tuning the model, or launching an explicit recovery attack. To mitigate this problem, we first characterize reappearing data points following unlearning and identify their distinct local loss geometry immediately after deletion. Even when the target itself satisfies the forgetting criterion, nearby points may remain recoverable, indicating that the model still retains strong denoising ability in its local neighborhood. We refer to this vulnerability as data-space recovery sharpness . Our analysis shows that targets that later reappear exhibit sharper post-deletion recovery geometry than those that remain forgotten, revealing an association between local recoverability and subsequent reappearance. This finding suggests that reliable unlearning should account not only for the observed target but also for locally recoverable representations that may preserve a route back to memorization. Motivated by this finding, we propose Low-loss Adaptive Search and Targeted Intervention in Neighborhood Geometry ( LASTING ). LASTING finds the most recoverable nearby representation and targets it during deletion. The search is repeated throughout optimization, allowing the method to expose and suppress the strongest remaining recovery route as the model changes. By aligning the deletion update with the identified recovery geometry, LASTING suppresses recoverable representations around the target, leading to more persistent forgetting. We evaluate LASTING over long sequential deletion trajectories, measuring immediate forgetting, reappearance over subsequent updates, and generation utility. Our results demonstrate that LASTING substantially improves forgetting persistence while preserving generation quality. Together, these findings show that successful diffusion unlearning requires forgetting to persist through subsequent deletion updates, rather than merely succeeding immediately after deletion.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce a target-level evaluation protocol for sequential diffusion unlearning that tracks whether each target is forgotten immediately and remains forgotten at the end of the sequence. • We identify sequential reappearance under ordinary deletion requests and find that targets that later reappear exhibit distinct local data-space recovery geometry immediately after deletion. • We propose LASTING , a recovery-geometry-aware unlearning method that adaptively identifies and suppresses the most locally recoverable representation around each target, and demonstrate that it significantly improves forgetting persistence over long deletion sequences while preserving generation utility.

sections.heading: Memorization in Diffusion Models
sections.text: Diffusion models are known to memorize individual training examples. Several studies have shown that generated images can closely resemble training samples, while extraction attacks have successfully recovered such memorized images at scale ( Somepalli et al. 2023a ; Carlini et al. 2023 ) . Subsequent studies have examined how factors such as data duplication, data coverage, and text conditioning affect replication and have developed methods for detecting or mitigating memorization ( Somepalli et al. 2023b ; Wen et al. 2024 ; Merger and Goldt 2026 ) . Other studies have proposed inference-time mitigation strategies, such as perturbing prompts associated with memorized outputs or modifying the initial noise ( Wen et al. 2024 ; Somepalli et al. 2023b ; Han et al. 2025 ) . Unlike these inference-time interventions, diffusion unlearning seeks to remove the influence of selected training examples from the model itself.

sections.heading: Diffusion Model Unlearning
sections.text: Diffusion unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training data or semantic content from a pretrained model, while preserving its utility on unrelated inputs. Unlike inference-time mitigation, which suppresses memorized outputs only during generation, unlearning modifies the model itself to provide a persistent removal effect.

sections.heading: Concept Unlearning
sections.text: Concept-level unlearning aims to suppress broad semantic content, such as objects, artistic styles, identities, or text-specified concepts. Existing approaches edit model weights, align target representations with anchor concepts, or select parameters according to their relevance to the target concept ( Gandikota et al. 2023 ; Kumari et al. 2023 ; Zhang et al. 2024a ; Fan et al. 2024 ) . Other methods extend concept erasure to selective or multi-concept settings ( Heng and Soh 2023 ; Lu et al. 2024 ; Li et al. 2025 ) . However, because deletion is defined at the semantic level, these methods cannot precisely remove a particular copyrighted or sensitive training data while preserving semantically related content.

sections.heading: Data-Point Unlearning
sections.text: Data-point unlearning aims to remove the influence of an individual training data point while preserving generation quality. EraseDiff steers the reverse process for a forget sample away from its original denoising trajectory ( Wu et al. 2025 ) . Subtracted Importance Sampled Scores (SISS) balances target forgetting and utility preservation through an importance-sampled score objective ( Alberti et al. 2025 ) . ReTrack redirects the denoising trajectory of a forget sample toward its k k -nearest neighbors in the retain set ( Shi et al. 2026 ) . More recently, Khalafi et al. (2026) formulate diffusion unlearning as constrained optimization based on forward or reverse KL divergence. Lee et al. (2026b) introduces a prompt-free instance unlearning approach that uses an additional generative model and edited surrogate targets to remove specific instances without relying on textual prompts. These methods offer complementary mechanisms for removing individual examples, but they primarily focus and evaluate on forgetting immediately after each deletion update. Our work instead examines whether an instance that is successfully forgotten at deletion remains forgotten as the same model undergoes subsequent deletion updates.

sections.heading: Recovery and Persistence after Unlearning
sections.text: Recovery after unlearning has mainly been studied under explicit post-unlearning interventions. Prior work has shown that erased concepts can be restored through limited fine-tuning using the removed instance ( George et al. 2025 ) . Meta-unlearning improves resistance to malicious relearning, whereas AdvUnlearn targets adversarial prompt attacks after unlearning ( Gao et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2024c ) . Our setting instead concerns spontaneous reappearance during ordinary sequential deletion, without any recovery attack, additional fine-tuning, or reuse of the removed instance.

sections.heading: Sequential and Continual Unlearning
sections.text: Recent work has examined sequential unlearning primarily for semantic concepts in diffusion models. Prior studies investigate cumulative utility degradation and propose regularization-, prior-preservation-, or locality-based mechanisms for maintaining retained generative capabilities across successive concept removals ( Lee et al. 2026a ; Thakral et al. 2025 ; George et al. 2026 ) . Closest to our setting, Zhang et al. (2024b) report an unlearning rebound effect in sequential style erasure, while Park et al. (2026) identify a related forgetting reversal phenomenon in continual classifier unlearning. However, sequential data-point unlearning in diffusion models remains largely unexplored. This setting is particularly relevant when copyright or privacy requests target individual training images and accumulate over time.

sections.heading: Parameter-space sharpness.
sections.text: Loss-landscape sharpness has been widely studied in relation to generalization and robustness ( Keskar et al. 2017 ; Dinh et al. 2017 ) . Methods such as Sharpness-Aware Minimization and Adversarial Weight Perturbation characterize the loss variation induced by bounded perturbations to the model parameters ( Foret et al. 2021 ; Wu et al. 2020 ) . Recent unlearning studies similarly operate in parameter space, seeking forgetting solutions that remain stable under weight perturbations or subsequent relearning ( Tang and Khanna 2026 ; Malekmohammadi et al. 2025 ; Fan et al. 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Data-space local geometry.
sections.text: Local geometry has also been studied in the input space of classifiers. Hsu et al. (2025) examine whether perturbed versions of a forget sample remain recognizable after unlearning, while AMUN uses nearby adversarial examples to reshape the classifier’s local decision boundary ( Ebrahimpour-Boroojeny et al. 2025 ) . In contrast, our work studies the data-space geometry of the diffusion denoising loss around an individual deleted training example. Rather than measuring parameter-space flatness or classifier decision-boundary robustness, we identify nearby image perturbations that remain easy for the diffusion model to denoise and relate this post-deletion recovery geometry to later sequential reappearance.

sections.heading: Reappearance under Sequential Deletion
sections.text: We first apply this protocol to sequences of K = 300 K=300 deletion requests using SISS, EraseDiff, ReTrack, Prompt-Free, and FU ( Shi et al. 2026 ; Wu et al. 2025 ; Alberti et al. 2025 ; Khalafi et al. 2026 ; Lee et al. 2026b ) . As shown in Fig. 1(b) , previously forgotten targets can return to the memorized regime as sequential deletions progress. This confirms that immediate forgetting does not necessarily persist through subsequent deletion updates and raises the question of why some targets reappear while others remain forgotten.

sections.heading: 4 Proposed Method
sections.text: In this section, we propose Low-loss Adaptive Search and Targeted Intervention in Neighborhood Geometry ( LASTING ), a recovery-geometry-aware method for sequential unlearning. LASTING searches for a low-loss neighbor of each deletion target and uses it in place of the original target when computing the deletion objective. By repeating this search throughout optimization, LASTING adapts the unlearning update to the model’s recovery geometry.

sections.heading: Experimental setup.
sections.text: We conduct our main experiments on CelebA-HQ ( Karras et al. 2018 ) using a pretrained 256 × 256 256\times 256 unconditional DDPM based on the formulation of Ho et al. (2020) . We consider sequential deletion trajectories of K ∈ { 50,100,200,300 } K\in\{50,100,200,300\} targets. At deletion stage i i , the model obtained after unlearning target a i a_{i} is passed directly to the next stage, such that all deletion requests are processed sequentially by the same model. Within each sequence length, the target order and retain set are fixed across the compared methods. Detailed optimization settings and hyperparameters are provided in the Appendix. sections.heading: Evaluation metrics.
sections.text: We measure target recoverability using the SSCD similarity ( Pizzi et al. 2022 ) between each deletion target and its reconstruction obtained through the reverse diffusion process. Immediate SSCD is measured at the target’s immediate model state θ i \theta_{i} , whereas Final SSCD is measured at the common final model θ K \theta_{K} . In both cases, lower SSCD indicates stronger forgetting. Following prior work, we set the SSCD threshold to τ = 0.7 \tau=0.7 and report Final Success and Reappearance Rate as defined in Eq. 2 . The reappearance rate is computed over targets that are successfully forgotten immediately after deletion and measures the fraction that return to the memorized regime under the final model. We also evaluate retain-side generation quality using FID ( Heusel et al. 2017 ) , where lower values indicate better quality. sections.heading: Sequential unlearning results.
sections.text: Table 1 reports target recoverability, forgetting persistence, and generation quality across different deletion sequence lengths. Although all baselines achieve substantial immediate forgetting, their performance degrades as subsequent deletion updates accumulate. At K = 300 K=300 , EraseDiff and ReTrack attain only 41.33 % 41.33\% and 39.33 % 39.33\% Final Success, with Reappearance Rates of 58.25 % 58.25\% and 56.27 % 56.27\% , respectively. SISS is more robust, but still reaches only 89.67 % 89.67\% Final Success with a 9.73 % 9.73\% Reappearance Rate, showing that strong immediate forgetting does not ensure persistent forgetting. In contrast, LASTING consistently improves forgetting persistence. At K = 300 K=300 , it achieves the lowest Final SSCD of 0.3917 0.3917 , the highest Final Success of 97.67 % 97.67\% , and the lowest Reappearance Rate of 2.33 % 2.33\% . Compared with SISS, it also reduces Immediate SSCD from 0.2807 0.2807 to 0.2281 0.2281 and Final SSCD from 0.4238 0.4238 to 0.3917 0.3917 . Similar gains are observed at K = 100 K=100 and K = 200 K=200 . LASTING also preserves generation quality, achieving a competitive FID of 24.81 24.81 at K = 300 K=300 , compared with 28.00 28.00 for SISS, 28.90 28.90 for ReTrack, and 75.70 75.70 for EraseDiff. Although Prompt-free Instance Unlearning obtains a lower FID, it suffers from a substantially higher reappearance rate.

sections.heading: Trajectory-level persistence.
sections.text: To assess forgetting stability throughout the full deletion trajectory, we also evaluate Ever Reappearance, defined as the fraction of immediately forgotten targets that re-enter the memorized regime at least once during subsequent deletion updates. As shown in Table 2 , LASTING achieves the lowest Ever Reappearance rate of 7.00 % 7.00\% , compared with 23.49 % 23.49\% for SISS and substantially higher rates for ReTrack and EraseDiff. This result indicates that LASTING preserves forgetting not only at the final checkpoint but also across intermediate deletion updates. Detailed results separating transient and final reappearance are provided in the appendix.

sections.heading: Extension to Text-Conditioned Latent Diffusion
sections.text: We further evaluate LASTING on Stable Diffusion v1.4, a text-conditioned latent diffusion model ( Rombach et al. 2022 ) . This experiment examines whether LASTING remains effective when deletion is performed in latent space and generation is conditioned on text.

sections.heading: Experimental setup.
sections.text: We construct a sequence of K SD = 49 K_{\mathrm{SD}}=49 memorized deletion targets using the prompts identified by Webster (2023) . Each target consists of a reference memorized image and two evaluation prompts: the original prompt associated with the memorized image and a modified prompt used to obtain a more diverse synthetic distribution. Following Alberti et al. (2025) , we generate 128 128 samples for each modified prompt to construct memorized and non-memorized example sets based on their similarity to the reference image. All 49 49 deletion requests are applied sequentially to the same Stable Diffusion pipeline and further implementation details are provided in the Appendix.

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol and metrics.
sections.text: At K ∈ { 10 , 20 , 30 , 49 } K\in\{10,20,30,49\} , we evaluate all processed deletion targets using their original and modified prompts. For each target–prompt pair, we generate 16 16 images with fixed random seeds and determine forgetting following the memorization criterion of Alberti et al. (2025) . Final Success measures the fraction of pairs forgotten under the checkpoint after K K deletions, while Reappearance measures the fraction of immediately forgotten pairs that later reproduce a memorized instance. We also report CLIP-IQA ( Wang et al. 2023 ) for generation quality. Representative qualitative results are shown in Fig. 3 .

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Table 3 shows that LASTING ’s persistence advantage extends to prompt-conditioned latent diffusion. It achieves no reappearance at K = 10 K=10 and remains competitive at K = 20 K=20 , with a Reappearance Rate of 2.70 % 2.70\% . The advantage is clearer for longer deletion sequences. At K = 30 K=30 , LASTING achieves 88.33 % 88.33\% Final Success with only 5.88 % 5.88\% reappearance, compared with 66.67 % / 22.45 % 66.67\%/22.45\% for SISS and 61.67 % / 31.25 % 61.67\%/31.25\% for EraseDiff. At K = 49 K=49 , it achieves the highest Final Success ( 93.88 % 93.88\% ) and is the only method with no observed reappearance. These results indicate that LASTING preserves forgetting under subsequent deletion updates rather than merely suppressing each target at its deletion stage. LASTING also maintains competitive generation quality while substantially improving forgetting persistence. The qualitative examples in Fig. 3 further show that memorized content remains suppressed at the final checkpoint without evident degradation in visual quality.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we identify sequential reappearance , a failure mode in which a diffusion training instance that is forgotten immediately after deletion becomes recoverable again after subsequent unlearning updates. Our analysis indicates that this failure is associated with sharper local recovery geometry around the deleted target. Motivated by this finding, we propose LASTING , which adaptively identifies and suppresses locally recoverable representations during unlearning. Across diffusion settings, LASTING substantially improves forgetting persistence while preserving generation quality. These results highlight the need to evaluate diffusion unlearning beyond immediate deletion success and to account for the stability of forgetting under subsequent requests.

sections.text: We conduct ablations on the number of inner-search steps J J , the neighborhood radius ϵ nbr \epsilon_{\mathrm{nbr}} , and the importance of the neighbor-selection strategy in LASTING . sections.heading: Appendix F Stable Diffusion Experimental Details and Results
sections.text: We provide additional implementation and evaluation details for the sequential Stable Diffusion experiments reported in the main paper. We describe the construction of the deletion sequence, the target-specific KMeans classifier used for memorization evaluation, the CLIP-IQA protocol, and the optimization settings for all compared methods. We then present additional qualitative comparisons at the immediate and final model states.

sections.heading: Data and Sequential Deletion Protocol
sections.text: We implement Stable Diffusion v1.4 using the Hugging Face Diffusers library ( Rombach et al. 2022 ) . We select K SD = 49 K_{\mathrm{SD}}=49 deletion targets from the fully memorized prompt–image pairs identified by Webster (2023) and use the data construction of SISS ( Alberti et al. 2025 ) . Each target contains one reference memorized image, its original prompt, a modified prompt, and 128 images generated from the modified prompt. Following ( Alberti et al. 2025 ) , we use target-specific KMeans classifiers to partition the generated images into memorized and non-memorized subsets. The memorized subset serves as the stage-specific forget set, while the non-memorized subset serves as the retain set. Across the 49 target partitions, this yields 6,272 images in total, including 3,108 memorized and 3,164 non-memorized samples. We order the 49 targets lexicographically and apply the deletion requests sequentially. The first stage starts from the pretrained Stable Diffusion v1.4 pipeline, and the model obtained at stage i i initializes stage i + 1 i+1 . Each stage uses only the forget and retain sets of its current target, while the updated model parameters are carried forward. All methods use the same target order, target assets, initial model, and checkpoint-transfer rule. We report the prefix checkpoints at K ∈ { 10 , 20 , 30 , 49 } K\in\{10,20,30,49\} .

sections.text: We evaluate memorization separately for the original and modified prompts and measure generation quality over their combined outputs. The protocol applies the main-paper persistence metrics to target–prompt cases using a target-specific KMeans classifier.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2609.25166v1 [cs.LG] 21 Sep 2026 Mitigating Sequential Reappearance in Diffusion Data-Point Unlearning Donghyun Kim Taehyuk Lee Jinyeong Kim Youngmin Oh Dohyeong Kim Jaehyuk Ryu Sangwoo Hong \corresponding Abstract Diffusion data-point unlearning is typically evaluated immediately after each deletion, even though subsequent requests may repeatedly update the same model. We identify sequential reappearance, a failure mode in which an instance that is initially judged to be forgotten later returns to the memorized regime without reuse of the deleted data or adversarial fine-tuning. To capture this behavior, we introduce a target-level evaluation protocol that tracks whether each target is forgotten immediately, remains forgotten at the end of the sequence, or reappears during subsequent deletions. We further find that targets that later reappear exhibit sharper local denoising-loss geometry after deletion than targets that remain forgotten. We characterize this vulnerability as data-space recovery sharpness and show that this post-deletion local geometry is associated with subsequent reappearance risk. Motivated by this finding, we propose a sharpness-guided unlearning method that iteratively identifies the most recoverable region around each target and extends the deletion objective to that region. Experiments show that our method improves forgetting persistence across long deletion sequences while preserving generation utility, highlighting the importance of evaluating diffusion unlearning beyond immediate deletion efficacy. Diffusion models can memorize and reproduce individual training examples, raising privacy and copyright concerns when sensitive data must be removed ( Somepalli et al. 2023a ; Carlini et al. 2023 ) . Diffusion data-point unlearning addresses this problem by removing the influence of a specific training instance without retraining the model from scratch ( Alberti et al. 2025 ; Shi et al. 2026 ) . A reliable deletion, however, should remain effective not only when it is performed but also throughout subsequent updates to the same model. As illustrated in Figure 1(a) , a target that appears successfully forgotten at its immediate checkpoint can become memorized again after later deletion requests are processed. Existing evaluations of diffusion unlearning ( Alberti et al. 2025 ; Wu et al. 2025 ; Shi et al. 2026 ; Park and Park 2026 ) predominantly assess each target at or near the model state immediately following its deletion. Such stage-local evaluation overlooks the target’s lifecycle under future model updates and can therefore overestimate deletion reliability. We identify sequential reappearance , a failure mode in which an initially forgotten target returns to the memorized regime as subsequent deletion requests update the model. Importantly, this failure emerges within the ordinary unlearning sequence, without reusing the deleted target, adversarially fine-tuning the model, or launching an explicit recovery attack. To mitigate this problem, we first characterize reappearing data points following unlearning and identify their distinct local loss geometry immediately after deletion. Even when the target itself satisfies the forgetting criterion, nearby points may remain recoverable, indicating that the model still retains strong denoising ability in its local neighborhood. We refer to this vulnerability as data-space recovery sharpness . Our analysis shows that targets that later reappear exhibit sharper post-deletion recovery geometry than those that remain forgotten, revealing an association between local recoverability and subsequent reappearance. This finding suggests that reliable unlearning should account not only for the observed target but also for locally recoverable representations that may preserve a route back to memorization. Motivated by this finding, we propose Low-loss Adaptive Search and Targeted Intervention in Neighborhood Geometry ( LASTING ). LASTING finds the most recoverable nearby representation and targets it during deletion. The search is repeated throughout optimization, allowing the method to expose and suppress the strongest remaining recovery route as the model changes. By aligning the deletion update with the identified recovery geometry, LASTING suppresses recoverable representations around the target, leading to more persistent forgetting. We evaluate LASTING over long sequential deletion trajectories, measuring immediate forgetting, reappearance over subsequent updates, and generation utility. Our results demonstrate that LASTING substantially improves forgetting persistence while preserving generation quality. Together, these findings show that successful diffusion unlearning requires forgetting to persist through subsequent deletion updates, rather than merely succeeding immediately after deletion. Contributions. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce a target-level evaluation protocol for sequential diffusion unlearning that tracks whether each target is forgotten immediately and remains forgotten at the end of the sequence. • We identify sequential reappearance under ordinary deletion requests and find that targets that later reappear exhibit distinct local data-space recovery geometry immediately after deletion. • We propose LASTING , a recovery-geometry-aware unlearning method that adaptively identifies and suppresses the most locally recoverable representation around each target, and demonstrate that it significantly improves forgetting persistence over long deletion sequences while preserving generation utility. 2 Related Work Memorization in Diffusion Models Diffusion models are known to memorize individual training examples. Several studies have shown that generated images can closely resemble training samples, while extraction attacks have successfully recovered such memorized images at scale ( Somepalli et al. 2023a ; Carlini et al. 2023 ) . Subsequent studies have examined how factors such as data duplication, data coverage, and text conditioning affect replication and have developed methods for detecting or mitigating memorization ( Somepalli et al. 2023b ; Wen et al. 2024 ; Merger and Goldt 2026 ) . Other studies have proposed inference-time mitigation strategies, such as perturbing prompts associated with memorized outputs or modifying the initial noise ( Wen et al. 2024 ; Somepalli et al. 2023b ; Han et al. 2025 ) . Unlike these inference-time interventions, diffusion unlearning seeks to remove the influence of selected training examples from the model itself. Diffusion Model Unlearning Diffusion unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training data or semantic content from a pretrained model, while preserving its utility on unrelated inputs. Unlike inference-time mitigation, which suppresses memorized outputs only during generation, unlearning modifies the model itself to provide a persistent removal effect. Concept Unlearning Concept-level unlearning aims to suppress broad semantic content, such as objects, artistic styles, identities, or text-specified concepts. Existing approaches edit model weights, align target representations with anchor concepts, or select parameters according to their relevance to the target concept ( Gandikota et al. 2023 ; Kumari et al. 2023 ; Zhang et al. 2024a ; Fan et al. 2024 ) . Other methods extend concept erasure to selective or multi-concept settings ( Heng and Soh 2023 ; Lu et al. 2024 ; Li et al. 2025 ) . However, because deletion is defined at the semantic level, these methods cannot precisely remove a particular copyrighted or sensitive training data while preserving semantically related content. Data-Point Unlearning Data-point unlearning aims to remove the influence of an individual training data point while preserving generation quality. EraseDiff steers the reverse process for a forget sample away from its original denoising trajectory ( Wu et al. 2025 ) . Subtracted Importance Sampled Scores (SISS) balances target forgetting and utility preservation through an importance-sampled score objective ( Alberti et al. 2025 ) . ReTrack redirects the denoising trajectory of a forget sample toward its k k -nearest neighbors in the retain set ( Shi et al. 2026 ) . More recently, Khalafi et al. (2026) formulate diffusion unlearning as constrained optimization based on forward or reverse KL divergence. Lee et al. (2026b) introduces a prompt-free instance unlearning approach that uses an additional generative model and edited surrogate targets to remove specific instances without relying on textual prompts. These methods offer complementary mechanisms for removing individual examples, but they primarily focus and evaluate on forgetting immediately after each deletion update. Our work instead examines whether an instance that is successfully forgotten at deletion remains forgotten as the same model undergoes subsequent deletion updates. Recovery and Persistence after Unlearning Recovery after unlearning has mainly been studied under explicit post-unlearning interventions. Prior work has shown that erased concepts can be restored through limited fine-tuning using the removed instance ( George et al. 2025 ) . Meta-unlearning improves resistance to malicious relearning, whereas AdvUnlearn targets adversarial prompt attacks after unlearning ( Gao et al. 2025 ; Zhang et al. 2024c ) . Our setting instead concerns spontaneous reappearance during ordinary sequential deletion, without any recovery attack, additional fine-tuning, or reuse of the removed instance. Sequential and Continual Unlearning Recent work has examined sequential unlearning primarily for semantic concepts in diffusion models. Prior studies investigate cumulative utility degradation and propose regularization-, prior-preservation-, or locality-based mechanisms for maintaining retained generative capabilities across successive concept removals ( Lee et al. 2026a ; Thakral et al. 2025 ; George et al. 2026 ) . Closest to our setting, Zhang et al. (2024b) report an unlearning rebound effect in sequential style erasure, while Park et al. (2026) identify a related forgetting reversal phenomenon in continual classifier unlearning. However, sequential data-point unlearning in diffusion models remains largely unexplored. This setting is particularly relevant when copyright or privacy requests target individual training images and accumulate over time. Sharpness and Local Geometry in Machine Unlearning Parameter-space sharpness. Loss-landscape sharpness has been widely studied in relation to generalization and robustness ( Keskar et al. 2017 ; Dinh et al. 2017 ) . Methods such as Sharpness-Aware Minimization and Adversarial Weight Perturbation characterize the loss variation induced by bounded perturbations to the model parameters ( Foret et al. 2021 ; Wu et al. 2020 ) . Recent unlearning studies similarly operate in parameter space, seeking forgetting solutions that remain stable under weight perturbations or subsequent relearning ( Tang and Khanna 2026 ; Malekmohammadi et al. 2025 ; Fan et al. 2025 ) . Data-space local geometry. Local geometry has also been studied in the input space of classifiers. Hsu et al. (2025) examine whether perturbed versions of a forget sample remain recognizable after unlearning, while AMUN uses nearby adversarial examples to reshape the classifier’s local decision boundary ( Ebrahimpour-Boroojeny et al. 2025 ) . In contrast, our work studies the data-space geometry of the diffusion denoising loss around an individual deleted training example. Rather than measuring parameter-space flatness or classifier decision-boundary robustness, we identify nearby image perturbations that remain easy for the diffusion model to denoise and relate this post-deletion recovery geometry to later sequential reappearance. 3 Analysis of Sequential Reappearance Protocol and Metrics Sequential unlearning setup. The qualitative examples in Fig. 3 further show that memorized content remains suppressed at the final checkpoint without evident degradation in visual quality. 6 Conclusion In this paper, we identify sequential reappearance , a failure mode in which a diffusion training instance that is forgotten immediately after deletion becomes recoverable again after subsequent unlearning updates. Our analysis indicates that this failure is associated with sharper local recovery geometry around the deleted target. Motivated by this finding, we propose LASTING , which adaptively identifies and suppresses locally recoverable representations during unlearning. Across diffusion settings, LASTING substantially improves forgetting persistence while preserving generation quality. These results highlight the need to evaluate diffusion unlearning beyond immediate deletion success and to account for the stability of forgetting under subsequent requests. References Alberti et al.
